Grade 4 · Unit 4.4

Structures, Senses, and Responses

How do body parts and senses help living things survive?

Every living thing is built with parts that help it survive. This unit covers the jobs of outside parts like roots, fur and beaks, the jobs of inside parts like hearts, lungs and plant tubes, and how senses gather information that the brain uses to guide a response.

A sense organ is a body part that gathers information, like eyes, ears, or skin.

In this lesson

  1. External structures have jobs
  2. Internal structures have jobs
  3. Senses send information and the body responds
  4. Try it at home
  5. Check yourself
  6. Play: Body Part Match

Concept 1

External structures have jobs

A structure is a body part with a job. An external structure is on the outside of a body or plant. An internal structure is inside.

Outside parts such as roots, leaves, fur, beaks, and spines help organisms get needs, grow, and stay safe.

Diagram

Plant structures

Roots, stem, leaf, and flower.

“Roots hold and soak up. Leaves catch light. Flowers help make seeds.”

Real world

Cactus spines

A cactus with spines.

“Spines help protect the cactus. Structures help survival.”

Try it

Structure match

Cards with structures and cards with jobs.

“Match the part to its job. Then argue: This part helps because…”

  • Root: holds the plant and soaks up water
  • Stem: holds the plant up
  • Leaf: catches light
  • Flower: helps make seeds
  • Spine of a cactus: protects the plant
  • Deer ears: hear danger

Cut the cards apart, mix, and match. Then say: “This part helps because…”.

Concept 2

Internal structures have jobs

Inside parts such as hearts, lungs, skeletons, and plant transport tubes help organisms live, grow, and reproduce.

Plant transport tubes move water and sugar inside a plant.

Diagram

Human inside

Heart, lungs, and skeleton.

“Your heart pumps blood. Your lungs take in air. Your skeleton supports you.”

Diagram

Plant stem inside

A stem with tiny tubes.

“Stems carry water and sugar inside the plant.”

Try it

Inside/outside sort

Structure cards sorted into inside and outside groups.

“Sort inside and outside. Then ask: What job does it do?”

Outside

  • Skin
  • Fur
  • Leaf
  • Spine of a cactus
  • Root

Inside

  • Heart
  • Lungs
  • Brain
  • Stomach
  • Tubes in a stem

Cards to sort: skin, heart, leaf, lungs, fur, spine of a cactus, stomach, brain, root, tubes in a stem. Put each card in Inside or Outside, then say its job.

Data

Argument frame

A claim is a statement you think is true. Evidence is what you saw or measured that supports it.

Sentence frame: “I claim ___ helps survival because ___.”

“Pick one inside structure. Use evidence.”

Worked example: “I claim the heart helps survival because it pumps blood to the whole body. My evidence is that without a pump, the blood would not move.”

Concept 3

Senses send information and the body responds

A reaction is how quickly your body answers something you notice.

Sense organs collect information, the brain processes it, and the body responds.

Diagram

Path model

Muscles are the body parts that pull to make you move.

Eye or ear → brain → muscles.

“Information goes in. The brain sends a response.”

Real world

Deer hears predator

A predator is an animal that hunts other animals for food. In Michigan, coyotes, bobcats, and black bears hunt deer fawns, and gray wolves hunt deer in the Upper Peninsula.

“A deer hears a sound. Its brain says danger. It runs.”

Hands-on · Design or investigate

Try it at home or in class

A fair test changes only one thing at a time. A reaction is how quickly your body answers something you notice.

This fair-test investigation asks, “Which sense gives a quicker response: sight or sound?” One student holds a ruler, and another student catches it when it drops. Students compare two ways to start the catch: watching the ruler with eyes open, and eyes closed with a sound cue (the dropper says “now” at the moment of release). The same two students keep ruler height and hand position the same, and the dropper lets go without warning, after a different secret wait each time and with no hint of when. They do 5 tries for sight and 5 tries for the sound cue, record every catch mark, and use the middle mark for each cue. They only say one cue is faster if the difference between the two middle marks is bigger than the gap between the tries at that cue. They write one claim with evidence. The sound cue also depends on how well the dropper times the word, so they say it is a rough comparison, then swap roles and see whether the result holds.

Try it

What you need

  • Ruler
  • Paper
  • Index cards
  • Tape
  • Crayons
  • Pictures of plants and animals
  • String (optional)

Safety: Drop only light rulers and keep feet clear. If using real leaves, soil, or outdoor samples, wash hands afterward.

Try it

What you do

Sort external and internal structures. Match structures to jobs. Build a sense→brain→response model. Test reaction distance with a ruler drop: 5 tries for sight, 5 tries for the sound cue, and use the middle mark for each cue.

  1. Sort structure cards into Inside and Outside and say a job for each (10 minutes).
  2. Match structures to jobs (10 minutes).
  3. Do the ruler drop: 5 tries with eyes open, 5 with eyes closed and a “now” cue (15 minutes).
  4. Write one claim with evidence.

Notice: The farther down the ruler you catch, the slower the response.

Why it matters: Body structures work together, from the senses to the muscles.

Data

Reaction data

Catch marks on the ruler for 5 tries with each cue, plus the backup dataset.

“Write each catch mark for 5 tries with sight and 5 tries with the sound cue. Circle the middle mark for each cue.”

Worked reading: Compare the middle marks, not single catches. Farther down the ruler means a slower response.

Backup dataset (3 tries for each cue, not 5):

  • Sight: 12 cm (about 4.7 in), 10 cm (about 4 in), 9 cm (about 3.5 in)
  • Sound cue: 14 cm (about 5.5 in), 12 cm (about 4.7 in), 13 cm (about 5 in)

The middle marks are 10 cm (about 4 in) for sight and 13 cm (about 5 in) for the sound cue. That gap is not bigger than the gap between the tries, so the backup data does not show that one cue is faster.

No time or no good weather? Use this data

No time or no good weather? Use the backup data in the Reaction data block above.

Near you: Michigan deer use ears and eyes to detect danger. Robins use their eyes, and maybe their ears, to find worms and bugs on the ground. White pines keep their needles all year, so they are evergreen. White pine is Michigan’s state tree.

Words to know

structure
a part with a job.
external
outside.
internal
inside.
sense
a way the body collects information, such as sight or hearing.
brain
an organ that processes information.
response
what the body does after processing information.
organ
a body part with a special job.
survival
staying alive.
model
a drawing or tool that shows how something works.
evidence
observations that support a claim.
Tutor notes: misconceptions and pacing

Pacing: five 30-minute sessions.

Common misconceptions to listen for:

  • “Only outside body parts matter.” Correct: internal structures have jobs too.
  • “Plant parts are just decorations.” Correct: plant structures help survival, growth, and reproduction.
  • “Plant parts are not real structures.” Correct: roots, stems, leaves, and flowers are structures with jobs.
  • “Responses happen without information.” Correct: senses collect information, the brain processes it, and the body responds.
  • “Senses and responses are the same thing.” Correct: senses collect information; responses are actions after processing.
  • “The brain is not part of the body’s response system.” Correct: the brain processes information and helps the body respond.

Limits and cautions:

  • Internal structures are simplified; cells and organ systems are not taught here. Those belong in later units.
  • Ruler-drop distance is evidence of reaction time, not an exact time measurement. The sound-cue version also depends on the dropper’s timing, so it is a rough comparison. Students do 5 tries per cue, use the middle mark, and say one cue is faster only if the gap between cues is bigger than the gap between tries.
  • Plant internal transport is simplified; the unit avoids xylem/phloem detail.
  • The unit does not cover inherited traits or ecosystems; those are in 3.3, 3.4, and 5.3.

Connections: Builds on: Unit 0: How Science Works; 1-B Parts, Parents, and Young; 3.4 Survival, Fossils, and Change. Builds toward: Unit 7 Cells; Unit 9 Body Systems & Homeostasis; Unit 8 Classifying Life.
